title: Skyscrapers and smokestacks: the grittier side of Georgia O’Keeffe
text:
Georgia O’Keeffe is celebrated for her ethereal depictions of flowers, sunlight, landscapes and animal bones, their gracefully swooping forms dripping with organic curves and seemingly on the verge of melting before our eyes. Such an approach would seem to be quite at odds with the firm, straight lines of farmhouses and barns, to say nothing of the electrified skyscrapers of New York City – and yet that is exactly what is centered in Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture, a new show at the Detroit Institute of Arts (Dia).
“I wanted to tell a new story about an artist who is so familiar,” said curator Ben Colman, who oversaw this collection of close to 40 works from the famed artist. “We can take a fresh look at works that O’Keeffe always considered essential and celebrate them in the way she wanted to.”
The idea for the show emerged from O’Keeffe’s 1932 work Stables, which is the only piece on exhibition that is in the Dia’s collection. It’s a charmingly tranquil side view of the titular construct, dominated by bright green, rich burgundy and subtly textured eggshell white, made by O’Keeffe during one of her many travels through the rurals of upstate New York and far-out parts of eastern Quebec. The artist regularly adventured through these rough and remote lands before deciding to leave New York City and live full-time in New Mexico in 1949.
Colman explained that Stables gave him the inspiration to look at O’Keeffe’s work with fresh eyes and seek out other ways of exploring her subtle textures and studies in pure color. “Stables is very precise in its use of geometry, and for many people who know O’Keeffe also a bit unexpected,” said Colman.
With his eyes attuned to the geometries of Stables, Colman began to seek out more and more of O’Keeffe’s architectural works. Among other things, this search let him put fresh eyes on to the artist’s New York City pieces, many of which she made from the vantage of her apartment window; she and her husband Alfred Stieglitz started on the 11th floor of the Shelton hotel in 1926, then moved up to the 28th, and finally the 30th floor out of 31. “It was likely the tallest residential building in the world at the time,” said Colman.
This high vantage let O’Keeffe create unprecedented cityscapes, among them a series of works depicting the gritty urban industrial life surrounding the East River. With smokestacks billowing out pollution and endless rows of nondescript urban buildings, it’s quite far from the works O’Keeffe is famous for, but according to Colman, in these pieces she’s honing her ability to represent the feeling of a place by the buildings that fill it, a talent that she would famously apply to New Mexico’s adobes in subsequent years.
“She tried very hard to represent the spirit and character of these places,” said Colman. “So in my mind it connects an adobe church in New Mexico with a skyscraper in midtown Manhattan.”
Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture also offers viewers a most remarkable depiction of the Brooklyn Bridge; verging on religious in its adoration of a beloved icon, it was made by the artist in 1949 as a sort of swan song as she was on her way out of New York. The piece is dominated by a flattened view of the bridge’s famous arches, bringing to mind the shapes of stained glass windows, framing gracefully swooping renditions of the bridge’s suspending cables. It neatly defamiliarizes the bridge, toying with abstraction while offering much to anchor the eye in reality.
“It’s a deeply personal painting,” said Colman, “documenting a moment of transition for O’Keeffe. It places our point of view into a moment of departure, and there’s a beautiful, poetic quality to how she uses light and variations of color, almost like looking through a stained glass window.”
Another noteworthy aspect of Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture is that it brings together multiple depictions of a humble patio door, a beloved part of the artist’s home in Abiquiu, New Mexico. O’Keeffe bought the house in 1945, taking four whole years to restore it from the ruined state that she found it in. It became her permanent home in 1949, and she resided there until 1984, just two years before her death.
The patio door paintings are a part of a suite of nearly abstract works centered around doors that O’Keeffe made during the 1940s and 50s, remarkable for the variety of colors that she brings to these simple, repeating forms. “Once she saw this patio door,” said Colman, “O’Keeffe decided that it was something that she needed to live with. She was inspired to paint it dozens of times, and it’s part of an extraordinary series of works, some of the most abstract in her career, but also so precisely anchored and placed.”
Placing her alongside contemporaries such as Agnes Martin and Mark Rothko, these pieces are color studies formed out of minimalistic geometries, generally showing rectangles of color with minimal, if any, perspective. After viewing one of the patio door paintings, Martin wrote to O’Keeffe: “It was a joyous experience and afterwards I knew more about the possibility of human response.”
Immersive digital experiences offered at the exhibition let audiences actually feel what it’s like to be in some of the places that O’Keeffe inhabited while painting – the upper floors of the Shelton hotel and her beloved patio in Abiquiu. They offer a chance to slow down and let one’s senses take charge, as museum-goers take their shot at attending to the subtle details of place that O’Keeffe drank in as she attempted to capture the pure essence of a location.
Colman is excited to be bringing O’Keeffe’s architectural works to light, a part of her career that is built on an entire social network of architects and designers that she had deep personal and creative relationships with. In his telling, it’s a story that has long resided in the archives, and now is the time to give it greater prominence in a celebrated artist’s career. “It’s a really exciting story,” he said, “to see these rich connections that inspired her to engage with the built environment for many years. I think visitors will be surprised that these works exist at all.”
- 
  Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture is on view from 11 September to 3 January at Detroit Institute of Arts
